locators_opened.evidence: The entry displays noun senses for suspicion of something on little or no evidence, being suspected of wrongdoing, distrust, and a minute amount/trace; it also marks the verb informal and gives the Middle English, Anglo-Norman/Old French, and Latin origin. Relevant lines 40–45.

The entry gives c. 1300 Middle English suspecioun via Anglo-French/Old French from Late Latin suspectionem (nominative suspectio), related to suspicere; it notes learned Old French influence on English spelling and the historical U.S. Western slang verb. Relevant lines 50–56.

The entry shows sə-ˈspi-shən; noun senses of suspecting wrongdoing, mental uneasiness/uncertainty comparable to doubt, and a barely detectable amount/trace; a chiefly dialectal verb; the suspicion/mistrust distinction; that-clause examples; the noun etymology; and a legal definition usually short of belief based on no or slight evidence. Relevant lines 31–56, 61–69, 90–116, 124–140, and 199–208.
The official release says a man was arrested on suspicion of breach of the peace and would be taken to a police station for questioning. Relevant lines 54–62.

The entry displays matching UK/US IPA forms, the word family, sense 1 with countability and wrongdoing/no-proof meaning plus on suspicion of and that-clause examples, sense 2 as a belief that something is true without proof, sense 3 as inability to trust, and sense 4 as a formal small amount with hint and a suspicion of a smile; it also gives the origin and under suspicion idiom. Relevant lines 97–120, 168–175, 207–215, 245–252, and 267–271.
